_doc: Pitch and info-panel facts. Each one is quoted or closely paraphrased from the URL given. Use only these in the pitch.

facts.text: At Mars' closest approach, about 35 million miles away, a signal takes about four minutes each way; when the planets are farthest apart it is around 24 minutes.

source.title: NASA Goddard: Space communications, 7 things you need to know

facts.text: NASA groups the risks of human spaceflight into five hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments.

source.title: NASA Human Research Program: The human body in space / five hazards

facts.text: Invisible to the human eye, space radiation is considered one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.

source.title: NASA Human Research Program: five hazards

facts.text: Approximately 69% of long-duration astronauts present with the earliest indications of SANS (a new sign in at least one eye during or right after flight: optic disc edema, chorioretinal folds, globe flattening or a refractive shift). NASA notes the severity threshold for pathological SANS is not yet known.
facts.qualifier: Long-duration astronauts; counts the earliest indications, not clinically significant disease. The team's 81% figure could not be confirmed on a nasa.gov or NTRS page and is not used.

source.title: NASA NTRS 20220000516: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS): Clinical Update

facts.text: NASA limits an astronaut's career effective radiation dose from spaceflight to less than 600 mSv, for all ages and sexes.

source.title: NASA OCHMO radiation protection technical brief

facts.text: Curiosity's RAD measured an average of 1.8 millisieverts of galactic cosmic radiation per day on the cruise to Mars.

source.title: NASA JPL: Data from NASA rover's voyage to Mars aids planning

facts.text: On the Martian surface RAD measured an average of 0.67 mSv per day (August 2012 to June 2013).

source.title: SwRI: first radiation measurements from the surface of Mars

facts.text: On the ISS, effective doses accumulate at approximately 0.2 to 0.5 mSv per day, about 40 to 90 mSv over a typical six-month mission.

source.title: NASA NTRS 20250006168: Moon 2 Mars Space Radiation Protection

facts.text: NASA-STD-3001 requires the one-hour average CO2 partial pressure in the habitable volume to stay at or below 3 mmHg; headaches are reported between 2.8 and 4.5 mmHg.

source.title: NASA OCHMO-TB-004 Carbon Dioxide

facts.text: Hypoxia symptoms can be mistaken for fatigue, and a crew member experiencing hypoxia may lose cognitive function and reasoning.

source.title: NASA OCHMO-TB-003 Habitable Atmosphere

facts.text: Aluminium and polyethylene shielding gives an average 50% reduction in dose from solar particle events, but only about 7% for galactic cosmic rays.

source.title: NASA OCHMO radiation protection technical brief

facts.text: NASA's VEG-04 study on the ISS grew mizuna mustard and surveyed crew before, during and after flight on plant care, to test whether tending plants supports behavioural health on long missions.

source.title: NASA NTRS 20205008589: VEG-04 Pick-and-Eat crop production and human research on the ISS

facts.text: A 2025 NASA poster on 27 astronauts who worked with the Veggie plant system concluded that working with and eating plants may serve as a behavioural health countermeasure for long-duration spaceflight.

source.title: NASA NTRS 20250000411

facts.text: Isolation and confinement is one of NASA's five hazards; NASA researchers are building ways to monitor behavioural health and to catch early risk factors in flight.

source.title: NASA HRP: Hazard - Isolation and Confinement

facts.text: The ISS carries medical packs (such as convenience and oral medication packs) listing each medication, its side effects and stowage location.

source.title: NASA ISS Medical Kit Checklist (2015 release)

head.title: Brain and cognition
head.what: Thinking speed, attention, mood and sleep.
head.spaceflight: Deep-space radiation, isolation, sleep loss and workload can all slow reaction time and lower mood. NASA tracks cognition and behavioural health on long missions.
head.next: Run the cognitive check and log mood and sleep.

source.title: NASA HRP: Hazard - Isolation and Confinement

head.how_to_measure: Here: the reaction test, and the mood and sleep log. On the station the neurological part of the physical exam is a standard functional exam and a gait exam, hearing is tested on orbit on or before flight day 21 and again about mid-mission, and each crew member has a 15-minute private psychological conference every two weeks.
head.why_it_matters: NASA lists the private conferences as one of the key elements of in-flight monitoring and countermeasures for behavioural health and performance. A slower reaction time or a lower mood is easier to act on when it is seen early.

eyes.title: Eyes and vision
eyes.what: Vision, and the back of the eye (optic disc and retina).
eyes.spaceflight: In weightlessness fluid shifts toward the head. About 69% of long-duration astronauts show the earliest signs of Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS). Tiredness and eye strain also show here.
eyes.next: Rest your eyes, and report any blurred vision to the flight surgeon.

source.title: NASA NTRS 20220000516: SANS Clinical Update

eyes.how_to_measure: Here: two questions in the guided exam (near vision, headache on waking). On the station the in-flight eye exam is vision testing (near and far acuity and an Amsler grid, about 20 minutes) with a questionnaire, plus fundoscopy, eye ultrasound, OCT and tonometry with a remote guider; six-month crews do it around flight days 30 and 90, 30 days before return, and when clinically indicated.
eyes.why_it_matters: The requirement exists to assess ocular health and function before, during and after flight, so a change in the eye is caught against the crew member's own preflight record.

heart.title: Heart and circulation
heart.spaceflight: Without gravity, fluids shift and the heart works differently; stress and poor sleep also raise resting heart rate.
heart.next: Try a slow breathing session (Orb Calm) and recheck.

source.title: NASA Human Research Program: five hazards

heart.how_to_measure: Here: heart rate from the camera, blood pressure from the cuff in the health log. On the station the crew medical officer runs a Periodic Health Status evaluation (vitals and a physical exam, about 15 minutes per crew member) with the blood pressure device from the medical diagnostic pack. A 12-lead resting ECG is recorded before and after flight, lying still for 15 minutes with 10 electrode sites. Veins are checked by ultrasound in flight (the internal jugular veins, the subclavian-axillary axis and the deep leg veins) around flight days 30 and 60 and six weeks before return.
heart.why_it_matters: The Periodic Health Status evaluation is how the crew's medical status is assessed in flight and reported to the crew surgeon; six-month crews do it at about two to three weeks, at 90 days and two to three weeks before return.

lungs.title: Lungs and breathing
lungs.what: Breathing rate and blood oxygen, and the air the crew breathes.
lungs.spaceflight: The cabin is a closed environment: CO2 builds up if scrubbers lag, and hypoxia symptoms can be mistaken for fatigue.
lungs.next: Check the cabin readout; if CO2 is high, move to a ventilated area.

source.title: NASA OCHMO-TB-004 Carbon Dioxide

lungs.how_to_measure: Here: breathing rate and blood oxygen, with the cabin air beside them. In NASA's physical exam the vital signs include the respiratory rate, and the chest and lungs are examined with the cardiovascular system; the in-flight Periodic Health Status evaluation repeats vitals and a physical exam.
lungs.why_it_matters: The exam before flight sets the record that in-flight checks are compared with, which is the same idea as Sentinel's change from your own baseline.

gut.title: Digestion and nutrition
gut.spaceflight: Far from Earth there is no resupply on demand: what the crew eats is planned months ahead, and fresh food is scarce.
gut.next: Log glucose after meals and note any nausea.

source.title: NASA Human Research Program: five hazards

gut.how_to_measure: Here: blood glucose in the health log, and nausea or appetite changes as symptoms. NASA's physical exam covers the abdomen by listening and by palpating the major organs, and the mouth and throat; abdominal ultrasound is one of the listed ultrasound examinations, and a dental check before flight asks about pain in the mouth and bleeding when brushing.
gut.why_it_matters: A dental or abdominal problem is far easier to correct before launch than on a mission, which is why these checks are scheduled well ahead of flight.

bones.title: Bones and muscles
bones.spaceflight: Without load-bearing, bone and muscle are lost in weightlessness; daily resistance exercise is the countermeasure. This build has no exercise sensor: the exercise log is DESIGNED, not running.

source.title: NASA Human Research Program: five hazards

bones.how_to_measure: Here: log back, joint or muscle pain by pointing at the body. NASA's physical exam checks the extremities for range of motion and general strength on a 1 to 5 scale, and the spine for general appearance and mobility.
bones.why_it_matters: Sore muscles change the findings: NASA asks that no strenuous exercise that leaves sore muscles is done in the 24 hours before a Periodic Health Status evaluation.

whole_body.title: Whole body: radiation
whole_body.what: Radiation dose to the whole body, and body temperature.
whole_body.spaceflight: NASA tracks cancer risk, central nervous system and cognitive effects, cardiovascular effects and cataracts from space radiation. You cannot feel it, so Sentinel shows it, and asks for the cognitive check so a trend is noticed early.
whole_body.next: Follow the storm checklist if an alert is raised; keep the cognitive check routine.

source.title: NASA HRP: five hazards (space radiation)

whole_body.how_to_measure: Radiation is modelled here, not measured on you. For the skin: photograph a cut, rash or allergic reaction when you notice it and again at intervals, so the healing can be followed.
whole_body.why_it_matters: NASA uses the photographs so flight surgeons can judge the extent and nature of a skin injury and monitor follow-up treatment, and to track how fast cuts and rashes heal in flight.

ISS Reaction Self Test: a 3-minute psychomotor vigilance test used as a fatigue flag
